studies.citation: Gornick M, Newton M, Hackerman C. Factors Affecting Differences in Medicare Reimbursements for Physicians' Services. Health Care Financ Rev. 1980;1(4):15–37.
studies.population: US Part B enrollees aged 65+; 1% analytic sample
studies.finding: Women/men, 1975 nominal dollars: mean reimbursement per enrollee $125/$140; deductible exceeded 51%/47%; mean allowed charge per service $14.60/$16.46. Inpatient surgery allowed charges reversed: $277.06/$267.94 (Tables 1, 3, 5).
studies.limitation: No diagnoses or specific procedure codes; incomplete below-deductible utilization. Service mix may explain differences. Historical customary/prevailing/reasonable-charge system; no causal or current-coverage inference.
studies.relevance: Historical patient-sex evidence on benefit distribution and cost sharing.
studies.extraction_level: Targeted full-text extraction; CMS PDF checked against indexed PMC
studies.identity_reporting: Enrollment-file sex; gender identity not reported.
studies.screening_notes: Population eligibility and risk-of-bias assessment pending; retain in historical synthesis separately from current policy.

studies.citation: Mauvais-Jarvis F et al. Sex and gender: modifiers of health, disease, and medicine. Lancet. 2020;396(10250):565–582.
studies.population: Clinical and preclinical literature; no Medicare cohort
studies.data_period: Search: Jan 2000–Jun 2020; earlier seminal work also cited
studies.finding: Synthesizes sex-related biology and gender-related social influences on disease, diagnosis and treatment. Provides a framework for evaluating clinical needs across disease domains.
studies.limitation: Selective narrative review; no original Medicare coverage, reimbursement or patient-cost analysis. Underlying studies require separate eligibility and quality assessment.
studies.relevance: Foundational clinical background for the national question and white paper; source for citation following.
studies.extraction_level: Targeted main-text review; citation and linked correction verified
studies.identity_reporting: Discusses sex and gender; no defined patient cohort. Not classified as cisgender-only.
studies.screening_notes: Linked correction L-B01-E1, PMID 32891210 (Figure 4 label). Retain background separately from direct reimbursement evidence.

studies.citation: Chang WH. Understanding the COVID-19 pandemic from a gender perspective. Taiwan J Obstet Gynecol. 2020;59(6):801–807.
studies.population: International literature on women and men; no defined Medicare cohort
studies.data_period: Early-pandemic literature, 2020; no formal search window reported
studies.finding: Discusses gendered caregiving, employment, occupational exposure and health-seeking behavior alongside early sex differences in COVID-19 outcomes.
studies.limitation: Author acknowledges limited source-credibility assessment, including non-peer-reviewed websites. Mixes early studies, preprints and media; clinical claims require independent verification. No Medicare reimbursement analysis.
studies.relevance: Background on social and economic pathways potentially affecting access; generates hypotheses for the national review.
studies.extraction_level: Targeted main-text review via indexed PMC; citation verified
studies.identity_reporting: Discusses men and women; no defined cohort or verified cisgender-only population.
studies.screening_notes: Underlying references require independent screening. No pooled estimate extracted; formal quality assessment pending.

studies.citation: Betron M, Gottert A, Pulerwitz J, Shattuck D, Stevanovic-Fenn N. Men and COVID-19: Adding a gender lens. Glob Public Health. 2020;15(7):1090–1092.
studies.population: Global public-health context; no original patient cohort
studies.finding: Highlights men's care-seeking barriers and gender norms. Proposes tailored outreach, shared caregiving and violence prevention, while acknowledging uncertainty about biological versus social drivers of COVID-19 risk.
studies.limitation: Commentary using prior research, programmes and media; no original cohort, systematic search or pooled effect estimate. No Medicare coverage or payment comparison.
studies.relevance: Framework for examining access barriers affecting either sex; Medicare applicability requires primary evidence.
studies.extraction_level: Publisher main text reviewed via indexed page; citation verified
studies.identity_reporting: Discusses men and women; no defined cohort or verified cisgender-only population.
studies.screening_notes: Publisher notes republication with minor changes that do not affect academic content. Cited interventions need independent retrieval and appraisal.

studies.citation: Tong A et al. Nephrologists’ Perspectives on Gender Disparities in CKD and Dialysis. Kidney Int Rep. 2022;7(3):424–435.
studies.population: 51 nephrologists, 22 countries (7 US); no patient cohort
studies.payer: Multiple health systems; no Medicare-specific analysis
studies.finding: Clinicians described caregiving, financial and transport barriers, limited support and stereotyping affecting women's kidney care. Men's provider roles and reluctance to relinquish control could also delay care. These are perceptions, not measured disparity rates.
studies.limitation: Purposive professional-network sample; English/German interviews. Responses reporting no perceived differences were not detailed. No patient interviews or Medicare payment, denial or cost estimates; national generalizability is limited.
studies.relevance: Original qualitative evidence for access mechanisms to investigate in CKD and dialysis; requires Medicare-specific follow-up.
studies.extraction_level: Targeted full-text review: methods, results, tables and limitations
studies.identity_reporting: Authors excluded transgender-patient disparity data. No patient cohort; clinician gender identity not established.
studies.screening_notes: Original research, not commentary. Retain as qualitative access context; formal appraisal pending. Linked editorial is a citation lead, not a correction.
